主要内容: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced on March 11, 2019, that 79 investment advisers had settled charges and returned over $125 million to investors, with a significant portion going to retail investors. The actions were part of the SEC’s Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative, launched in February 2018, aimed at addressing conflicts of interest in mutual fund share class selection. The initiative encouraged advisers to self-report violations of the Advisers Act, compensate investors promptly, and ensure proper fee disclosures. The SEC found that many advisers failed to disclose conflicts of interest when selecting higher-cost share classes, even though lower-cost options were available. These advisers were found to have received 12b-1 fees, which are recurring fees deducted from fund assets, without adequate disclosure to clients. The SEC emphasized that investment advisers, as fiduciaries, must fully disclose material conflicts of interest, including those arising from financial incentives, and act in the best interest of their clients. Since 2013, the Commission has charged advisers for failing to disclose such conflicts, requiring disgorgement and penalties, and distributing funds to affected clients. The SEC Share Class Initiative returned over $125 million to investors by addressing disclosure failures by investment advisers. These failures harmed retail investors, particularly by depriving them of the ability to make informed investment decisions when purchasing higher-cost share classes. The initiative, managed by the Asset Management Unit, allowed advisers to avoid financial penalties if they self-reported undisclosed conflicts of interest, compensated harmed clients, and corrected their disclosure documents. The SEC staff continued to evaluate self-reports received before the initiative cut-off date. SEC Chairman Jay Clayton emphasized the fiduciary duty of investment advisers to act in their clients' best interest. The initiative improved disclosure quality and returned funds to retail investors. Settlement terms found advisers violated Sections 206(2) and 207 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 by failing to disclose 12b-1 fees and additional compensation. Advisers agreed to cease-and-desist orders, censure, disgorgement, and distribution of funds to affected clients. The Commission agreed not to impose penalties under the initiative. The SEC Share Class Initiative has returned more than $125 million to investors. This initiative, led by Dabney O’Riordan, Chief of AMU, and coordinated by SEC Assistant Director Jason Burt, along with attorneys and industry experts, aims to ensure fair treatment of investors. The settlements announced today involved numerous financial firms, including Ameritas Investment Corp., AXA Advisors LLC, BB&T Securities LLC, and many others. The initiative is part of the SEC's broader efforts to enhance transparency and protect investor interests. The Division of Investment Management and the Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations have played significant roles in supporting this initiative. The initiative is part of the SEC's ongoing commitment to regulatory oversight and investor protection.
